utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam Registrar. If you could kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am. All the accused are present. From the Defence teams I only notice the absence of Mr. Lazarevic. The Prosecution is Mr. McCloskey, Mr. Thayer and Ms. Janisiewicz. The witness, Mr. Dibb, is presents in the courtroom. We will proceed with his testimony. I take it there are no preliminaries and then after that we'll continue with the other witness. Good morning to you, Mr. Dibb.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic will conclude his cross-examination soon. We'll then see if there is re-examination or whether there are any further -- but I don't think there are further cross-examinations so -- and hopefully within the next hour, you'll be out and free to go back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning Mr. Dibb.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, yesterday we left off essentially looking at Exhibit 1D00374 and with the Court's permission I'd like to give that exhibit to you again to review. But my question is specific. If you can just identify the individual on the front cover sheet, who was supposed to report to General Smith on or about July of 1995, with respect to the contents of what's in this document.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we got to yesterday, from Ken Biser drafted by Ed Joseph. What I would say, though, is that it's on the info list, it is purely up to the civil affairs chain, not necessarily through the military chain.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And Can you explain why it doesn't go through the military chain?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not particularly apart from the fact that we touched yesterday on command structures and if there are two parallel commands, in this case one civilian, one military, there is always the possibility that things will go up one and not necessarily up the other simultaneously.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And it would cause for more chaos or more disorder, would you agree?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly it's far from ideal but it also depends on what is the content of the document, and you would also have to ask General Smith rather than me as to just how much of this traffic he saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you because we were discussing the purported massacre that you heard although you don't remember from whom or when you heard it, was it at all possible or probable that you understood this massacre to be that they were Muslims who were killed during a combat battle while they were in the column trying to escape and leave Srebrenica to get to Tuzla or other BiH territory?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. My recollection is that the information we were receiving was that it had been an atrocity rather than a military action.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: As you sit here you don't know from whom you heard this from, nor when you heard it, correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: My recollection is it was certainly before deployment to Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, that's July 25th, I recall you saying, right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the earliest --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you hear if anyone died --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly request that the speakers make pauses between question and answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you recall if there was any news of any Bosnian Muslims dying as a result of combat operations while they were fleeing Srebrenica through the forest trying to reach the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this stage, sorry, no I don't recall if we had that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let's look together at this Exhibit 1D0 -- I lost the number now, but I think you could read it for me right on top, 374, I believe, up on the top right-hand corner?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, 374.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let's look at the second page of that document and although you were with Ed Joseph and other civil affairs officers from July 25th, with whom you may have had some informal if not formal discussions about the events that were developing both in Tuzla and around Srebrenica, do you see under bullet point number 3 under the caption "Some of the Srebrenica men arrive," then as we've discussed, they talk about the 5.000 or 6.000 who crossed into the BiH 2nd Corps territory and then the third bullet points talk about those who were killed?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down for the interpreters, thank you. Could counsel please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, do you see the third bullet point on page 2 which is captioned "Some of the Srebrenica men arrive"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No I'm looking in the wrong place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Dibb. Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, what we have up on e-court is not from what I can see what's being discussed. I don't know if anybody else is having this problem. Okay. We've got it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it is the one, okay. All right. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Maybe I'll restate it a little slower, Mr. Dibb.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, I know you're looking through the entire document, and you're welcome to look at it, but am I clear that you weren't giving these documents in preparation for your testimony by the Office of the Prosecutor, correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: This one I don't recall seeing before, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And this is a document I just want to you focus on the first paragraph of page 2 and it's under the caption where it says "Some of the Srebrenica men arrive." Do you see that on --

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, got it. Sorry, I was looking further down.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's okay. Paragraph number one, there is a three little hash marks, I'm focusing now on this third one. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've seen, yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, from the 17th, which is the date of this document, up through the 25th and while you were in Zepa with Mr. Edward Joseph, did you ever or do you recall discussing that there were men who were killed on the way through the forest trying to escape Srebrenica to reach the free territory as they called it?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall discussing that with them, but I also don't see anything peculiar that I've failed to recall that. We may well have discussed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, as you sit here, you don't recall it, though, correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And do you remember discussing the number that was being reported by the UNMOs, the civil affairs, and others?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that being discussed at this stage. However, again, things have slightly mashed together over time. What I do recall is that it -- information came out in bits and pieces and there was over a period of some time. There's debate over what the numbers were.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you remember a debate about whether the number was greater than or less than 3.000?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not particularly, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We get information that you had maintained some notes or records during your stay in the former Yugoslavia, and I know you said that it could be in several different places. Had you ever had an opportunity to go back and try to find those notes?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have seen them before. What has happened since is I've moved out of Scotland to Afghanistan and packed my stuff up, so they are somewhere I'm just not sure where.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Have you done anything recently to try to obtain or uncover those notes?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I've not been back in the U.K. for months.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What I find interesting here, you work with the Halo Trust and obviously you're in charge or you have a directorship position with a company that does de-mining projects across the world, correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a directorship but yes, I'm one of the senior staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: One of the senior staff. Hopefully one day you'll be director, but with respect to that do you see in this specific bullet point that the UNMOs, the civil affairs, and other United Nations organisations reported that these men were killed among other reasons as a result of mines that were placed in the forest over the course of the three years in the war?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Wouldn't that be an interesting point for you as a person who works with the Halo Trust to look at and to examine and to find out whether it's -- how accurate it is?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I'm allowed to speculate I'd say thousands killed on mines is a fantasy.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And why is that?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: It just simply mine casualties don't get that high over quick periods of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Share with me this: How many mines were placed in the forest through -- from 1992 to 1995 on the route that the column took from Srebrenica to Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I simply don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, you worked for the Halo Trust, do you know if anything at the Halo Trust did any such investigative work to determine that?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We, the Halo Trust did -- we call it a recce into Bosnia, but we chose not to work there. What I can say is that mine figures globally tend to be hugely exaggerated, and I think at one stage there was talk of 33 million mines being laid in the former Yugoslavia possibly in Bosnia itself. Again, I would say without hesitation that would be a fantasy. We've is seen countries such as Afghanistan, people talk about 10 to 15 million. Having been there for 20 years, I would say the number is closer to 620.000 and that statistical difference is something that we have seen in virtually every country we have worked in around the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you explain or can you tell us if there is any reason that the facts that are set forth in this internal cable, which is highlighted as being immediate and restrictive with the United Nations, is there any reason that we should disbelieve these three or other points that they make in this table?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: You've got to look at the date on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The 17th of July 1995?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah and you've got it think how long it takes to gather that sort of information, and I don't doubt that they were getting reports coming in to say these things had happened. However, there is obviously absolutely no time at all to - I would say - to verify whether these things had actually happened. And if we are talking specifically on the issue of mine accidents, which I'm extremely familiar with, that would take you know weeks if not months I think to ascertain genuinely if that many people were injured on mines on that particular route.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, as you sit here, do you know if any UN organisation or entity actually tried to find the answer to that question? It's been 12 years now.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm well aware that is a Bosnian mine action centre run by the UN who I would assume have done some sort of survey work, but having said that, and with due respect, I've got, how to phrase it, not the greatest respect for UN-run mine action centres around the world. So they may or may not have done that, and you would have to speak to them and consult records which must be on the public record because donors who fund mine action surveys, one of the criteria of providing the funding is that that information is public information.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, we are not just going to look at the mining accidents or incidents that may have occurred but it also references BSA engagements. Do you see that immediately after the word, I think, "mines"?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know what BSA stands for, Bosnian Serb army?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many BSA engagements there were from the fall of Srebrenica up through this report, the 17th of July 1995?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have absolutely no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So you never discussed that with Edward Joseph?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again I can't say I did or didn't discuss it. I would also say sitting here that Edward Joseph and anyone in civil affairs would also not have none exactly how many engagements there were. They might have had a knowledge of how many reported engagements but that too wouldn't necessarily be the definitive amount.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You spoke a little bit about Captain Bliss, I think, do you remember his first name who was your counterpart to the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Emma Bliss.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know if he prepared similar such reports while he was negotiating or speaking with the ABiH representatives at that time?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, Emma is a she but that's beside the point entirely.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if she would have -- if she had been in meetings with senior BiH officers and that information had been passed to her, then I have little doubt that she would have passed that information on to General Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, who would have been providing information that General Smith so that he could find a balance between what his people are telling him the Bosnian Serbs are doing and that which the Bosnian Muslims were doing at that critical time? Would it have been Captain Bliss?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly, but I would guess it would have been happening at a - and again I stress I would guess - it would have been happening at a higher level and it wasn't -- it wasn't rare for General Smith's office to be contacted by Mr. Muratovic and his office. And he would call up the general and say, "Listen, these are the reports that are coming to us." So it wouldn't necessarily have been through BiH military channels. It could have been through Muratovic's office. And in such cases, it's-- I've certainly attended meetings with Muratovic that General Smith attended. I'd have thought it was as likely or more likely that he would have gone in person to such a meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, do you know who was in charge to actually determine from the ABiH army or ABiH being the army, the number of soldiers that were fleeing from Srebrenica? Do you know who the one individual was that was supposed to maintain that information or gather that information?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, just to clarify the person within BHC staff tasked to gather that?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a J2 intelligence cell as part of that -- as part of BHC setup so that sort of information would -- the primary source of that would have come through the J2 cell rather than the two liaison officers, myself and Captain Bliss.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Would you give me a name of a JC officer that would have been providing that information as to how many Bosnian Muslims were potentially in the forests and breaking through and ultimately reaching the free territory?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again that information must be readily available. I'm trying to remember the man's name, it might have been Paul but I might be completely wrong on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, you talk a little bit about the disorder that UNPROFOR experienced in Tuzla on or about the 14th of July when you were there. Can you tell me what in your view is the number 1 reason for this disorder?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a -- it's difficult to say exactly what the number 1 reason was. I think they were not as well prepared for it as they should have been, is self-evident. But whether that's the reason or whether that's a symptom of something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Was there any problems with actually the civilian population that was arriving in Tuzla that caused this to become more of a disorganised or disorderly assemblence such as rocks throwing by the people who arrived, whether we call them displaced persons or refugees?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I recall at that stage. It wouldn't surprise me at all if tension had built up and rocks may have been thrown at a later date. However, that -- if that happened, again, I surmise that would have been because not enough was being done in the short term, so I think it was more a failing on the UN and other bodies to get themselves organised which was the problem. And probably the sheer scale of the people coming in. Again Tuzla hadn't, I don't think, was -- I don't know how well staffed Tuzla was at that stage, but it was more down to their inability to deal with it than a problem with the refugees/displace.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now you mentioned earlier today Mr. Muratovic, who was minister I think, is it Dr. Hasan Muratovic, do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hasan Muratovic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And do you remember if there were any conflicts between the United Nations and him in particular being a representative of the BiH with respect to the refugees that had just an arrived on the days that you were there, do you remember that at all?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I don't and what I would say is that for quite a bit of this period I was as we've noted in Tuzla, Bratunac, and Zepa itself which means to some extent I was out of the whatever conflict was going on within BHC command itself. So things would almost certainly have been going on that wouldn't have been part of my immediate patch or day to day dealings over this period.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Help me with this. What was Mr. Muratovic's main purpose and goal, if you remember, at that period from the 14th on of 1995, July?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where I remember clearly Muratovic's name coming up was when we were in Zepa, so to be clear, I don't recall Muratovic's involvement from the 14th to prior to the 25th. I do remember his name coming up in Zepa in discussions of prisoner exchanges, and at that stage, there was I think two things. One it appeared that there was an effort to thrash out an agreement on the ground with the commanders on the ground, Avdo Palic, Mladic, saying with Palic being happy to say please look after my troops I'd like to get into a prisoner swap with the ABiH troops from Zepa, and BSA prisoners, the word coming back from Sarajevo was more hang on we want to do an all for all. And again I'm -- all for all, I'm surmising he means all ABiH prisoners, but at this stage I don't remember. Muratovic also slightly, I think once the main body of people had left, this whole issue of there is still civilians left in Zepa was again something raised by Muratovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But do you remember, sir, that in fact it was Muratovic who disagreed with Palic and did not want to exchange the purported 2.000 Bosnian Muslims soldiers who were in the hills with 500 VRS soldiers? Do you remember that at all?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's -- I remember that being the issue. What I can't tell you is how Muratovic's message was conveyed to that meeting, but I recall General Smith was attending the meeting so again, we would need to ask General Smith if he had met with Muratovic and had conveyed that message from Muratovic to that body, to the best of my knowledge, there was no direct communication between Avdo Palic and Muratovic, and we certainly weren't providing that communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well then I just need a little help. Even though you've read your statement before testifying and we're pretty clear on your recollection, it states on page 4 of your statement that Mladic wanted to exchange -- and you talked here in this statement which is on page 4, the first full paragraph on the 26th of July. It says that "Mladic wanted to exchange all the men from the hills in Zepa some 2.000 men for approximately 500 VRS prisoners being held by the Bosnians." You go on in your statement to say quote "Palic agreed to this but Muratovic would not agree." Where would you get that information if you're inviting me to ask General Smith but you had no such information but yet put it in your statement?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm -- what I'm saying is that would have been we talked yesterday with you or your colleague behind about did I have discussions with General Smith in Zepa, which I said almost certainly but I don't remember the content thereof. Obviously, I would have talked with Smith and Baxter, who I think probably was there, and there would have been some briefing on you know this is the situation that we are in so that we would have had awareness of what was happening around us. So I would say I've got that information from the Sarajevo team which turned up in Zepa to conduct these discussions with Mladic and Palic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But as you sit here, do you recall Muratovic not agreeing to that proposal by Mladic to make an exchange of 500 VRS soldiers for 2.000 Bosnian Muslim soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. If you're asking do I remember that being the issue, very definitely I do. If you're asking do I remember Muratovic personally saying it, very definitely I don't because I simply wasn't there when he did say it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But it's in your statement and there is no doubt that it was Muratovic who refused it, would you agree with me there?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: From my understanding, very definitely. I was absolutely clear in my mind that it was Muratovic who was the call it the stumbling block, call it whatever, in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Was this something that that you had experienced with the minister Muratovic prior to this occasion on July 26 involving Zepa or was this the first time that you experienced this as you coin it stumbling block?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, exact dates are difficult. I said earlier I had a meeting with Muratovic with General Smith. I think that probably happened sometime after this, but I know he was in fairly regular contact with General Smith and his office. And he's saying he was a stumbling block, let's put that in inverted commas. All sides were coming to us with their side of the particular story, and it was for the commander of UNPROFOR to try and steer a course through various sides so --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was the minister, Minister Muratovic particularly, was -- and this POW issue, would we call this a policy issue or how would you coin it?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Difficult for me to answer in that I don't think I'm -- well, I know I wasn't fully aware of all the facts surrounding it. I'm not sure if it was a Muratovic personal issue or if it was an issue where he truly represented the Bosnian government and it was something that had been agreed by General Delic and others, which I would have thought would have been relevant in this particular case.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But the POW issue is a policy issue, you would agree with me there, correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: The government policy or Muratovic policy?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Government policy in general.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really couldn't say on that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know if he was in a position, being a minister, whether he was in a position to make decisions relating to any government policy, whether it be POW or others?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a minister I'm sure he would have been, but can you remind me of what, minister of what that he was?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, actually many different roles, but I'd like to -- do you think General Smith, since you have found or think that Muratovic, Hasan was a person of position and prepared to make decisions relating to policy, do you know if General Smith would have had the same view as you did?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I was going to intervene not to let him answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, do you remember a person by the name or nickname Palijan [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Mustafa Hajrulahovic, do you remember him at all, an intelligence officer?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I know the name, Captain Bliss used to deal with him. I don't recall meeting him personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, during your proofing session with the Office of the Prosecutor, did you ever ask them for any documents that may have been generated or prepared by Captain Bliss or anyone to see what the ABiH was thinking in these critical moments from July 14th through the 25th, let's say?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Did they share with you any of the contents of those documents if any?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, I couldn't help but notice in reading your interview, you don't mention in your interview that you at -- by the 25th of July 1995, had received this information regarding a massacre but you testified to it here. When is it that you recalled that you remembered that you were informed of this massacre prior to July 25th 1995?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've said before, I don't have a clear recollection of that, of the date that it was informed, and what I'm absolutely clear on is we --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, who is the we?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: BHC.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Go ahead?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: BHC had suspicions something had happened, I simply, as I said, things have merged. So the dates that we became certain there had been a massacre versus the date there was consistent reports that something had -- was untoward had occurred, and I'm certain by the 25th if we hadn't had absolute confirmation there had been a massacre we were receiving consistent reports that something was amiss, and it was for that reason BHC took a decision to send a different team to Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me just show you one last document with the Court's permission, it's 2D0003, and I just have a couple of questions, Mr. Dibb, on this document and if the usher would be kind enough with your permission, Mr. President, to -- I guess we could just see it on e-court. Thank you. And again, Mr. Dibb, this is an out-going cable which seems to have some immediate status to it, and you could see to whom it's going and from whom and the people who are copied on this document. The date is the 19th of July 1995. Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just have a quick look at it. I don't remember seeing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. We just want going to focus your attention in the brief time that we have, it's a paragraph number 4 do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've only got half of hour at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's that half that I'd like to discuss with you, but you're welcome to take the original and look at both of them simultaneously if you would like.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you get a chance to look at that?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With respect to paragraph number 4, who from the United Nations was providing or was -- let me strike that and let me repeat it. From whom in particular was the United Nations representative obtaining the information that's reflected on paragraph number 4?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be perfectly honest, I'm not sure. The J2 cell at BHC may have been providing some of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's Paul again, right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, if that's the right man. Some may have been coming through that. Again it's coming up through the civilian chain not the military chain, so they may have been looking at other sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well look at the third sentence which is in the third line, doesn't it really indicate that it's a civilian source versus military when it starts the sentence by saying, "ABiH 2nd Corps report"? That seems to be more of a military source, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: It appears to be, but you also have to understand that everybody there was living this environment as you guys are living this particular case, and it wouldn't surprise me particularly if civilians were aware of which battalion was where. There are a lot of bright people out there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: There is no doubt about that, but what I'm wanting to actually obtain from you is, and if you don't know just tell us, would you know who the one individual who was with the ABiH 2nd Corps who would have been providing this information to the United Nations representatives?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know if these numbers could have been inflated or underrepresentative of what was really coming through?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd say certainly they -- it's possible, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Either way it's possible, correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And it's probable that it was depending on whether you had any political motivation to dictate other policies with respect to the ongoing war, wouldn't it? It's something that happened at that time, wouldn't you agree?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Looking at the previous document of mine casualties, I would say that figure was inflated. But it's possible but I would be speculating.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I want to go back to the mine thing only because I want to have you rest comfortably. There was never a statement that said 3.000 died as a result of any mine accidents. I think it was both the mine accidents as well as the BSA engagements?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Agreed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So we don't know just by looking at that whether it was 50 per cent mine accidents or 90 per cent mine accidents?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Agreed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Now we were talking a little about utilising some of this data for political purposes, and even if you look at the paragraph 4 towards the end of that paragraph on page 2, there seems to be some indication?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down for the translation? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And I do apologise. Just trying to get it within the estimated time, but I will slow down and I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dibb, we were generally talking about the use of such data which is highly relevant and critical, especially given the situation at that time and abusing that data for political purposes, okay, so focusing on that, do you know, sir, what if anything General Smith did to obtain more precise figures as to the number of ABiH soldiers who made it to the free territory?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't specifically, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you take any proactive initiative to obtain that information?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personally?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably not, no. We -- what General Smith did do was send Colonel Coiffet accompanied by me to Tuzla and down as far as Kladanj, where I'm certain we would have been asking ABiH personnel there what the story was. Thereafter, I was tasked on other different tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that there should be reports from people such as Colonel Coiffet and Powell from the JC 2 indicating what the ABiH may have told them as to the number of military or civilian men that reached Tuzla or Kladanj or any other area as a result of the fall of the Srebrenica enclave?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether they -- whether reports to Smith would be written, how much was done on briefs, again, the people who would know better than me. I think in situations like this there would be a blizzard of information coming in, or disinformation as we discussed coming in, and it would then be for people to sift through it. And it's as your man Rumsfeld said, you're dealing with all sorts of different knowns and unknowns, and any commander or indeed this Court are dealing in that same world of truths and half truths and trying to work out where exactly what you can count on and what you can't count on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Last section, if you will. Can you help me understand, and then you called it a morning prayers and these briefings, these are daily morning briefings that you and General Smith and others would attend, correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, the first one was a more -- the first one was a more general briefing which had various people from come commanders from all the outlying all the units within Sarajevo called in, would get a central ops brief in the morning, this is what we know, this is what's happened, this is what's going on. They would then often then be a slightly smaller forum afterwards discussing other issues, and sensitive intelligence matters would be more likely to be a face-to-face. As I said, I didn't have secret clearance, so I certainly wouldn't have been invited or, you know, again, why would I have the ability to attend those.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting that you did. Just give me an idea of how many people attended these morning briefings sessions, 8, 12?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the first one I would say more like 30, 40, the second one more like 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The second one is the meeting that follows the early morning meeting, correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And that would be broken down to 8, basically 8 people in one group, correct??

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: 8 is a random number, but a much smaller number.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just identify for me, if you will in your group that you were with, after their initial meeting meaning the group of 8, General Smith was with you, I take it?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, usually.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Who else, just if you can identify them and their position?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Smith, Colonel Baxter, and then really it would depend and again I'm scratching my head to remember if this smaller one was an every day or just when something had been raised. I would attend some, Coiffet as deputy Chief of Staff, Nicolai's Chief of Staff may or may not have attended. People from J2, J3, which is intelligence and operations, may or may not have attended.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And J3 is operations, right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And who was the person if you remember when was in charge of J3?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't, to be honest.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But there should some in some other documents, correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And is that the individual that you think most likely worked with the ABiH in determining exactly what if any kind of operations were undergoing in the forest while the men from Srebrenica were trying to make it to Tuzla or Kladanj?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I would say J2 would be the more appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: More intelligence than operations?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. That's all I have, Mr. Dibb.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ostojic. Do you have a re-examination, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I do have a few questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Forgive me, but I think I forgot to ask you what rank you held during these events in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a captain at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. You were asked yesterday by Madam Fauveau about a statement you gave to the OTP, Office of the Prosecutor, in 2006, and that's at page 16299 of yesterday's transcript. The statement refers to a meeting you had on September 19th with General Smith, General Dragomir Milosevic of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, and General Miletic. Just to be clear, do you recall whether the investigators and the attorneys from the OTP who interviewed you in 2006 were part of this case or part of some other case?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment before you answer. Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really do not see the relevance of this question. I don't see that the answer of a witness really depends on the team to which the Prosecutor belongs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's your answer to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour it very well may be relevant, if certain teams don't know certain players, don't know certain roles, they may not have an opportunity to realise that certain things are said or not being said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We see validity in the point you raised or you referred to in your answer to Madam Fauveau's objection. We agree with you, Mr. Thayer, so the witness now will proceed to answer the question if he's in a position to answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm afraid I was guilty of not digging into that team specifically at the time, so I couldn't answer for certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, sir, and do you remember the first time or any other time that you were interviewed by the Office of the Prosecutor and if so, do you recall what year that was?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time I was interviewed was, I believe, the end of 1996 in London.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, Mr. Josse asked you some questions yesterday about what information you had about the fate of the Srebrenica men by the time you left Zepa, and certainly that's been the subject of some questions by my friend Mr. Ostojic yesterday and today. I want to show you a couple of public-source articles that appeared during this period of time. We do have 65 ter numbers for them. The first is 65 ter 467, and we will be looking at page 2 of the English and page 2 of the B/C/S. Can you read that okay, can you read that all right, sir?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you blow it up a little bit?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. It's a little small on our screen, too.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You'll note that the source is Belgrade SRNA, the date is 17 July, the time is 1854 hours Greenwich mean time. There is a reference here to a Jovan Zametica and it describes him as an adviser to the president of the Bosnian Serb Republic. You referred to an individual, I believe, by a similar or identical name. Do you believe that this is the individual who you dealt with on the civilian side of the Serb government, sir?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, I just ask to you take a moment and read the article here.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, the -- apparently this appears to be a statement that Mr. Zametica --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'd like to know whether we could have the B/C/S version so that the accused can follow what is going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I do have hard copies, Mr. President, if that will be of immediate assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we have solved that, Madam Fauveau. Yeah, I think we have solved that Madam Fauveau. If at any time we need to go back to the English text and have it blown up again, we will do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, this appears, this article appears to be based on an a statement that was issued by Mr. Zametica and in it it refers to over the past few days the world media, assisted and prompted by the Muslim authorities, have indulged in an orgy of uncritical reporting on the events in Srebrenica, claims of torture, executions, rapes and deportations of Muslims are being constantly repeated without any independent confirmation. My question is, during this period of time, and I know you've told us that you were busy, you were assigned to other things, but did you become aware yourself, do you have any recollection of the international media raising these issues reporting on these reports of torture, executions, rapes and deportation to the extent that this individual with whom you liaised obviously felt compelled to issue a response? Do you remember the international media having picked up on these reports during this period of time?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do and again it's just trying to pinpoint at exactly which date I remember it happening but, yes, I remember that the media getting hold of the story pretty early on. And running with it ever since.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, if we could turn to 65 ter 466, and we'll be looking at page 3 of the English and page 5 of the B/C/S. And if we employ the same procedure that Mr. President suggested, I have a copy of the English for the witness if we are going to put the B/C/S on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just take a moment, sir, and let me know when you've had an opportunity to read it.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, this is a copy of an article that was picked up by the Beijing Xinhua. Do you know what that is, what the Xinhua News Agency is, sir?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Apparently it made it to China, and it refers to the UN Security Council on the 14th of July demanding that the Bosnian Serbs respect fully the rights of the civilian population from Srebrenica. Did you become aware during this period of time, sir, that in fact the UN had taken this action this early and that it had apparently been picked up by the international media? Is this the type of thing that you were aware of?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of the UN engaging and as you say dealing with demands for troops to move, for civilian population to be treated in a humane manner. I may be wrong in my recollection, but I seem to think there might also have been a civilian shot dead in front of the Dutch peacekeepers at that stage which I think was pretty well reported. And again that would have acted as a trigger anywhere that things weren't quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, sir, I just want to show you one other document along these lines, and this is not something that has a 65 ter number. It was disclosed 18 October of 2005. I have hard copies for all the parties, if they wish, and I've got a copy for the ELMO, just a couple of questions on it. The ERN is R0033695 to 3698. And do you have a copy? If you could please just look at the first -- the cover page and I'm only really going to ask you about one portion of one paragraph, so...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters do not have a copy of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: There should be sufficient numbers, so I would kindly ask someone to furnish -- okay. And we are putting it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, sir, the -- the document is dated the 13th of July, and it appears to be or is signed by General Smith; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Headed "The aftermath of fall of Srebrenica." If we look at the cover sheet, the distribution sheet, can you help us and just tell us based on this, can you tell what the scope of the distribution was meant to be for this document?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: HQUNPF Zagreb would be General Janvier. Attention SRSG, attache, FC, DFC, not sure, immediately Chief of Staff, COS, Chief of Staff, Brigadier General Nicolai.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And could FC and DFC stand for force commander and deputy force commander or is that not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: A leading question, and I object.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I mean, Mr. President --.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can rephrase it, Mr. Thayer, that's easy.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Were you aware, sir, of any abbreviations for General Janvier's position?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Janvier was, yeah, force commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'll move on to my question. Sir, I want to turn your attention to the first page of General Smith's memorandum and specifically to paragraph 3. Where it says, "The Bosnian Serbs are cleansing Srebrenica, DutchBat are doing what they can to monitor the situation but reports of abductions and murder unconfirmed as yet are beginning to be heard." Sir, let me ask you first, do you have any recollection of receiving or viewing this memorandum from General Smith?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, no, I don't remember specifically seeing this previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Were you aware at the time that General Smith had this type of information, these reports, that he refers to, and I'll leave it there for now?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, going back, as I've said, information was coming in from a variety of sources and my recollection is clearly that we were receiving reports of atrocities happening in and around Srebrenica, so, yes, I'm certain General Smith will have had those reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, my last question is: With respect to the negotiations that were on going with respect to Zepa and in particular to the disposition of the military-aged men of Zepa, my friend Mr. Ostojic asked you some questions about, for example, Minister Muratovic's role in those discussions. Did you ever become aware of the Bosnian Muslims fear, whether it was the Bosnian Muslims in Sarajevo, in the political area, or the Bosnian Muslims on the ground in Zepa, did you ever become aware of their fear of the military-age men of Zepa being placed, should there be a surrender, in the hands of the Serbs prior to any exchange versus in the hands of another party, for example, UNPROFOR, and that being an obstacle in the eyes of the Muslims, an obstacle to an agreement? Did you ever become aware of that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I can say -- and I may ask to you rephrase the bit about how it becomes an obstacle an agreement -- but let me answer part of it any way. When we spoke to Avdo Palic on the first day, he made it clear, and again, obviously his exact words I don't recall, but it was we hope that our troops or our people are going to be treated humanely, and what I do recall is my -- my interpretation of that being not -- not like what has happened previously in Srebrenica. We also have to look at the-- the means through which military-age men were evacuated from Zepa. It was quite clear the rest of -- women and children were put into unprotected buses and trucks but that simply wasn't deemed acceptable, I think by everybody, probably everybody meaning UN and Palic and the Bosnians themselves, and it was deemed that the military-aged men had to travel with UN drivers in armoured vehicles, which clearly shows there was genuine fear that something -- something might happen untoward if military-aged men fell into the hands of the Bosnian Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And then just to finish up on the question, and I'll try to clarify it for you. I know it was a convoluted question to begin with, but that concern that you just described of military-aged men falling into the hands of the VRS, do you recall hearing, receiving any information, that that concern became an obstacle to the overall or any overall agreement with respect to the military-aged men who were still in the hills; that is, whether the men would ever be placed in VRS hands or not during the course of any future exchange? Do you remember hearing anything about that? If you didn't, that's fine and that's my last question, sir.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. I simply don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, sir. I have no further questions?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Thayer. Mr. Dibb, we've come to the end of your testimony. There are no further questions for you, which means you're free to go. On behalf of the Tribunal I wish to thank you for having come over to give evidence and on behalf of everyone present, I wish you a safe journey back to your place of work.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, in an effort to meet the estimate I had given, I cut out all the video so as I'm sure everyone noticed. So we are really down to four items, the first is 65 ter 2575, P02575. The two press articles, P0 -- I guess that would be P00467 and P00466. Mr. President, I would offer what is -- we may have to have some discussions with my friends about this, but in the Krstic case there was a collection of news articles that reached the international press during this period of time, as we've seen. It has become an issue. Those were collected into an exhibit and admitted in the Krstic case. They do have all 65 ter numbers. They're all along the same lines as these two that I showed Mr. Dibb. We would offer that collective binder or small packet of documents along the same lines as Mr. Dibb's testimony showed their relevance today. We can put those together and have them ready to offer from the Bench. We'll certainly let our friends know, but I just want to let you know that that is an offer that will be coming based on the examination that we had with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But has the collection been already circulated as such amongst the --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: It's in e-court. They have the following 65 ter numbers so my friends can look at them at their leisure. They all have French and B/C/S translations already as they were a prior exhibit. Those 65 ter numbers are 465, 466, 467, and 468.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take it that you're giving notice of this. You're not tendering this document today, are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I think at this point, Your Honour, it's probably futile.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think they need to have -- I suppose each one of the Defence team has been taken by surprise like we have and -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I am taken by surprise, and I'm surprised at the way my learned friend is going about this frankly. As he is at pains to point out, rightly on occasions, there is reasonably good channels of communication between the parties in this case. And I'm sorry for putting it like this, but he could have had the courtesy to inform us of this in advance so that he would have had some idea what our response would have been. So at this particular juncture, we are certainly not in a position to agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm going to put a stop to it here now. Mr. Ostojic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: It's an invitation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, please sit down. We'll deal with this if ever you table an oral or written motion after having given time to the Defence teams to ponder about it and come to a conclusion. But we shouldn't lose -- waste more time on it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we stick to the documents that he mentioned, Mr. Thayer mentioned earlier. I haven't got the numbers in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: They are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's okay. Any objections? Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, the two newspaper articles, we would rather were adjourned until such time as this full collection is put before us. Your Honour, we recall that the Trial Chamber has had some reservations in the past about the admission of newspaper articles, and of course this can open a rather large potential Pandora's box, and in our submission, the matter would be better left to consider whether --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But these newspapers or reports were used with this witness. So I think one can isolate them from the rest, from the would-be collection that Mr. Thayer was referring to and which are pleasures yet to come.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I have nothing more to say about that, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If I can put a question to Mr. Josse, whether he can see a distinction between these two situations, one newspaper is a hearsay for the truth of the content of it, and the other as a non-hearsay for the proof of a certain article that appeared in that item.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, of course, I see that distinction. I've two observations. The first is if a newspaper article is only going in for the latter purpose, for the witness's reaction or to explain other evidence the witness might have given, then that really does need to be stated at the time in my submission, so the parties know where they stand so far as that is concerned because unless it's stated at the time, the matter is unclear and unclear when we come to make our final submissions in this particular case. My second comment in relation to these newspaper articles in general is of course this witness had no knowledge of either of these articles and nor frankly did they jog his memory to any great degree, and of course, it does really rather open the floodgates for newspaper galore to be introduced to witnesses in the way my learned friend has done in re-examination. Those are my observations, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Josse. Any further -- yes, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I would join my learned friend Mr. Josse in objecting to the newspaper articles, but I hope that this criminal court doesn't want to try the case on newspaper articles. This in particular is a witness who had some rather insightful views and was involved in some very important meetings, as we will see, with other witnesses that come in. I would hope that my learned friend would invite us and say we'll share the collection of all the out going and in going cable material that we have in our possession from both the Serb side as well as the Muslim side. We haven't heard that offer, but we see that they do have from time to time additional documents which don't have or bear the 65 ter number which was this one from Mr. Smith. I think it's more important for this Court to look at the facts as they existed from the principal parties than from what political or lobbyists were trying to convey to the media at that time. I would strongly urge that the Court reject these articles specifically given that Mr. Dibb did not acknowledge that he read them, that he relied on them, or even knew about it based on both the direct and the cross-examinations that were conducted. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ostojic. Mr. Thayer or any other Defence team wishes to contribute? No, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Sorry. Just before my learned friend replies could I ask, is he seeking to put in the Smith document at this stage?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I think it's relevant to a specific issue that the Defence raised very consistently during their cross-examination. It wasn't something that we had anticipated putting in, but to the extent that we've heard a lot of examination about the level of knowledge of these reports, for the same reason that these press articles are relevant because in fact this witness did say, yes this is the type of information that we were hearing. Yes, I remember the international press was all over this issue, they were reporting it from very early on and then consistently thereafter. The witness's testimony in fact was very clear on that issue, and the relevance of these articles, and I would submit the other articles that we've told our friends about, is clear. So I would offer this UN document to go to that specific issue that the Defence raised. Now, if it doesn't come in now, I'll make the decision whether it's something that General Smith may speak about and if -- and we'll just have to cross that bridge, but it's been raised by the -- by my friends, I don't see what the excitement is about. It's an issue that they went into, and it's an issue that is dealt with in the articles and in the memo itself. It's crystal clear that they are discussing reports of atrocities and murders and rapes and deportations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I address the Court on that document specifically if I may? I find it surprising in the extreme that that document was not on the 65 ter list. I am aware of the Trial Chamber's rulings in relation to the ability to put documents in in re-examination, and I certainly don't want to go behind that or revisit that particular issue but, Your Honour, the relevance of this issue, the issue as to the state of knowledge of UNPROFOR people at the time of the Zepa events, was gone into to some extent with Mr. Joseph, and in particular Judge Prost asked a question which alerted us to the importance of the issue and that is one of the reasons why we explored it with this particular witness. Now, Your Honour, my learned friend chose not to. It would be churlish and absurd of me to suggest that document, the Smith document, is not relevant to your considerations, and I don't say that for one moment but what I do say, yet again, is it is rather extraordinary that it wasn't on the list and the way it's now being used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Josse. So let's go through the documents one by one. The first one is P2575. Any objection to that? It is admitted. Now, then we have the two press articles, P -- correct me if I'm wrong, P467 and P466, correct? And these are being objected to by at least two Defence teams. One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So these two, having discussed amongst ourselves the unanimous position is that since they have been used with this witness, they are to be admitted and then the same applies to the Rupert Smith document, which doesn't have, regrettably doesn't have a 65 ter number, as rightly pointed out by Mr. Josse. Its reference ERN number is R 0033695 to 698, both numbers included. Now, let's start with Madam Fauveau. Do you have any documents that you wish to tender?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: There are three in a list that's just been distributed, Your Honour. 6D164 which was a report from Colonel Baxter, 6D166 which was the order from Mladic of the 30th of July of 1995. That translation of which has been received today, I can tell the Trial Chamber. And the third document, I'm in the Chamber and the registrar's hands as to how to cope with this, that's 2D125. I'm uncertain whether that's been admitted in whole. If it has, the question is why it hasn't all been translated, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My information is that it has been admitted with previous witness Trivic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Trivic, he's not protected, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, with Trivic. That's the information. Madam Registrar will check will whether it was admitted in toto or what's the question. However, as you indicated, when you made use of this document, there are still three pages that remain -- the three pages that you made use of remain untranslated.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, they do, Your Honour, and I suspect large parts of it remain untranslated. I'm the last person to ask for unnecessary translation work. We only need those three pages translated. I'm entirely in the Chamber's hands as to what to seek -- what should now happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Josse. Any objections from any of the Defence teams?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: One others observation, just a -- I said 6D164 at line 9 of page 38. It says 166. I'm sure that will be corrected in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Any objections from anyone? Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the first one is being admitted, is being marked for identification because we still don't have a B/C/S translation of it. Is that correct, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We -- the first one is in English, Your Honour. The second document we have a translation today, and it's the third one, I beg your pardon, the Trivic diary we don't have a translation of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But the first one we do have because the original is in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But we don't have a B/C/S version of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We don't need a B/C/S translation, and indeed we won't be provided one. The translation service will not provide us with such a translation, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So that is admitted, 6D166 is admitted, translation has arrived. And 2D125, if these three pages, as I understand, have already been admitted with previous witness Trivic, there is no point in admitting them again. Unless you specifically ask to select them and have them admitted separately, but I don't think --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No, I'm not asking for that. I repeat the issue of the translation of the whole of that document is something I'll discuss with the learned registrar if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So there is no point in marking anything for identification. We are just making an order for these three pages to be translated, and they will of course form an integral part of what is already Exhibit 2D125. Okay. Having said that, Mr. Haynes, I think we might as well take the break now. We've still got three or four minutes for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Certainly. And particularly given, as I understand it from others behind me, that there are preliminary matters that they wish to raise. I don't suppose there is even time to raise them in the next two minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Who wishes to raise preliminaries? Yes, Mr. Bourgon? Can you dispose of this in three minutes or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would prefer to have a few minutes simply to discuss with my colleagues so that we do have a common position rather than to go with only three teams, but this can be done very shortly at the beginning of the next session in a matter of ten minutes at the most and then we can put it to rest while the witness continues his testimony. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So we'll have a -- do you need more time than the 25 minutes? That should be more than enough. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The number that will be given to the Rupert Smith document is PIC 181. 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Shall we go into closed session? Yes, Mr. Bourgon. Let's go into closed session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 17th day of October, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.45 p.m.,
